newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan says China interferes HK shipping talks.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan says China interferes HK shipping talks.

text.p: Taiwan on Monday accused rival China of interfering with proposed talks on shipping links between the island and Hong Kong, saying Beijing's pledge to grant autonomy to Hong Kong was "nonsense".

Taipei, eager to work out crucial technical issues before the British colony's July 1 absorption by communist China, proposed on April 16 to host semi-official talks on shipping links with Hong Kong at the end of April.
Hong Kong has yet to respond to the proposal.

Taiwan's state-funded Central News Agency quoted Kao Koong-lian, vice-chairman of the cabinet's Mainland Affairs Council, as saying that China had prohibited Hong Kong negotiators from coming to Taiwan for talks.
"This shows communist China's so-called 'one country, two systems' and 'let Hong Kong people rule Hong Kong' are nonsense," Kao said.
Kao added that Beijing had "deliberately interfered" with talks between Taiwan and Hong Kong. He did not elaborate.
Under Sino-British handover treaties, the territory of 6.4 million people is promised a high degree of autonomy for 50 years, except in foreign affairs and defence.

Taiwan has authorised Chang Liang-jen, deputy secretary-general of the semi-official Straits Exchange Foundation, to hold talks with Hong Kong Shipowners Association chairman George Chao, Beijing's designated negotiator.

Hong Kong is the channel through which more than US$30 billion worth of Taiwan investments have poured into China since the late 1980s, when a political thaw unleashed an explosion of unofficial Taiwan-China ties.
Taiwan has warned of painful consequences if no deal is reached over Taiwan's crucial shipping links with Hong Kong -- including a possible halt to bilateral sailings.
At issue is what flags ships should fly when plying routes between Taiwan and Hong Kong.

Hong Kong's post-handover constitution states that after July 1, Hong Kong-registered ships on international routes must fly communist China's flag along with the territory's own Hong Kong Special Administrative Region flag.

Kao has said Taipei would welcome ships flying the red five-star of the communist People's Republic of China -- but only if Beijing and Hong Kong tolerated vessels that flew the flag of the exiled Republic of China on Taiwan.

China regards Taiwan as a renegade province and refuses to recognise the Republic of China, which has ruled the Nationalist redoubt since losing the mainland in a civil war in 1949 and fleeing to the island.

To avoid the sensitive sovereignty issue, Taipei proposes that both Taiwan and Hong Kong ships lower all flags and identify themselves through telex communications before entering each other's waters.
Neither Beijing nor Hong Kong's government-in-waiting has responded to the proposal.
Taiwan, which has banned direct links with China since 1949, has agreed to allow limited direct shipping with the mainland.

Under its scheme, mainland cargoes are not allowed to enter Taiwan customs but can be processed at the island's southern Kaohsiung "offshore transshipment centre" for onward passage to third countries.
On Sunday, the second ship to sail directly to Taiwan from China in 48 years entered the southern Kaohsiung Harbour complying with a requirement to fly Taiwan's Nationalist Republic of China flag.
The first ship to sail directly to Taiwan reached Kaohsiung on Saturday night without flying the flag.
